--- course-unit: ch12-sensitivity-and-identifiability status: complete --- # Sensitivity and identifiability {#sec-sensitivity-and-identifiability} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 2, Session 4. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd). ::: Sensitivity analysis asks how much a chosen model output changes when an input changes. Identifiability asks a different question: can the data, in principle, distinguish the parameters or only a combination of them? Keeping those questions separate prevents a common mistake in epidemic modeling: treating a precise numerical estimate as evidence that every biological parameter is learnable. ## Learning goals By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - distinguish local sensitivity analysis, global sensitivity analysis, and structural identifiability analysis; - compute local state sensitivities with the current [SciMLSensitivity.jl API](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/); - use a small Sobol analysis with [GlobalSensitivity.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/GlobalSensitivity/stable/); - use [StructuralIdentifiability.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/StructuralIdentifiability/stable/) to expose a parameter combination that observations cannot separate; and - validate a sensitivity calculation against conservation and a finite perturbation. ## Model assumptions and classification We use the homogeneous SIR model from @kermack1927. It is a deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population model. Individuals move irreversibly from susceptible to infectious to removed; the population is closed, well mixed, and has frequency-dependent transmission. The contact rate and per-contact transmission probability are kept as separate inputs even though the ODE depends on their product. With $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $N=1000$, contact rate $c=10$, transmission probability $\beta=0.05$, and recovery rate $\gamma=0.25$, the basic reproduction number is $\mathcal{R}_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$. Because $S(0)/N=0.99$, the initial effective reproduction number is $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{eff}}(0)=\mathcal{R}_0 S(0)/N=1.98$. These values are the course baseline. ## Equations Let $x(t)=(S(t),I(t),R(t))$. The transition rates are $q_{\mathrm{inf}}=\beta cSI/N$ and $q_{\mathrm{rec}}=\gamma I$: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt} &= -q_{\mathrm{inf}},\\ \frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt} &= q_{\mathrm{inf}}-q_{\mathrm{rec}},\\ \frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dt} &= q_{\mathrm{rec}}. \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-sensitivity-sir} The local sensitivity matrix is $J_x(t)=\partial x(t)/\partial\theta$, where $\theta=(\beta,c,\gamma)$. If a scalar quantity of interest is $z=h(x(t),\theta)$, then a first-order perturbation is $\Delta z\approx \nabla_\theta z\,\Delta\theta$. This approximation is local: it is informative near one parameter vector, not across an entire plausible range. Structural identifiability is about the observation map, not the solver. If only incidence $y=\beta cSI/N$ is observed, the transformation $(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,c/a)$ leaves the transmission term unchanged. Therefore $\beta$ and $c$ cannot be separated without additional information or an informative design. ## Julia implementation The course module provides the baseline constructors and plotting theme. The right-hand side below is written out as a pedagogical three-parameter kernel so that the derivative in @eq-sensitivity-sir is visible in the code. Note one departure from the named-tuple convention of @sec-julia-essentials: parameters travel here as the plain vector `p0 = [β, c, γ]`, unpacked positionally. Sensitivity analysis differentiates *with respect to the parameter vector*, so `ODEForwardSensitivityProblem` and `gsa` both require an indexable container whose column order defines what the derivatives mean. Where that is not forced, as in every chapter so far, prefer the named tuple. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using EpiModelingCourse using GlobalSensitivity using Logging using ModelingToolkit using OrdinaryDiffEq using SciMLSensitivity using StructuralIdentifiability baseline = BASELINE_PARAMETERS u0 = Float64[ BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.S, BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.I, BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.R, ] N = baseline.N p0 = [baseline.beta, baseline.contact_rate, baseline.gamma] tgrid = collect(0.0:1.0:40.0) function sir_kernel!(du, u, p, t) β, c, γ = p S, I, R = u incidence = β * c * S * I / N du[1] = -incidence du[2] = incidence - γ * I du[3] = γ * I return nothing end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` sir_kernel! (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ### Local sensitivities `ODEForwardSensitivityProblem` augments the original ODE with the variational equations. `extract_local_sensitivities` returns the state trajectory and a Jacobian for each saved time. This is the forward-sensitivity route in SciMLSensitivity; adjoint methods are preferable when there are many parameters but only a few scalar outputs. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} local_problem = ODEForwardSensitivityProblem( sir_kernel!, u0, (first(tgrid), last(tgrid)), p0, ) local_solution = solve( local_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = tgrid, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9, ) local_states, local_jacobians = extract_local_sensitivities( local_solution, true, ) final_jacobian = local_jacobians[end] final_jacobian ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3×3 Matrix{Float64}: -12339.5 -61.6977 2224.96 -1549.63 -7.74813 -26.0357 13889.2 69.4459 -2198.92 ``` ::: ::: The rows of `final_jacobian` correspond to $S$, $I$, and $R$, and its columns correspond to $\beta$, $c$, and $\gamma$. These three columns must not be compared directly, because each is measured in the units of its own parameter. The model depends on $\beta$ and $c$ only through the product $k=\beta c$, so $$ \frac{\partial I}{\partial\beta}=c\,\frac{\partial I}{\partial k}, \qquad \frac{\partial I}{\partial c}=\beta\,\frac{\partial I}{\partial k}, $$ {#eq-sensitivity-chain} so away from their common zeros their ratio is $c/\beta=200$. A raw plot therefore shows a $\beta$ curve two hundred times larger than the $c$ curve; that is a statement about the units in which each input happens to be measured, not evidence that $\beta$ matters more. Rescaling each derivative by its own parameter value removes the arbitrariness. The elasticity $$ E_j(t)=\frac{\theta_j}{I(t)}\,\frac{\partial I(t)}{\partial\theta_j} $$ {#eq-sensitivity-elasticity} is dimensionless: the fractional change in $I(t)$ per fractional change in $\theta_j$. Scaling by $\theta_j$ alone, without dividing by $I(t)$, does the same job in units of people rather than percent. Plotted either way the $\beta$ and $c$ curves coincide exactly, which is the same confounding that the structural analysis below derives symbolically. ::: {#cell-fig-ch10-local-sensitivity .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} infectious = local_states[2, :] raw_sensitivities = [[jacobian[2, j] for jacobian in local_jacobians] for j in 1:3] elasticities = [p0[j] .* raw_sensitivities[j] ./ infectious for j in 1:3] fig = Figure(size = (900, 420)) raw_axis = Axis( fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "∂I/∂θⱼ", title = "Raw derivatives (unit-dependent)", ) elasticity_axis = Axis( fig[1, 2], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "(θⱼ/I) ∂I/∂θⱼ", title = "Elasticities (dimensionless)", ) parameter_labels = ["β", "c", "γ"] parameter_colors = [:steelblue, :darkorange, :seagreen] parameter_styles = [:solid, :dash, :solid] for j in 1:3 lines!( raw_axis, tgrid, raw_sensitivities[j], label = parameter_labels[j], color = parameter_colors[j], linestyle = parameter_styles[j], ) lines!( elasticity_axis, tgrid, elasticities[j], label = parameter_labels[j], color = parameter_colors[j], linestyle = parameter_styles[j], ) end axislegend(elasticity_axis) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch10-local-sensitivity .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Local sensitivities of the infectious state. Left: raw derivatives, whose relative sizes are fixed by the units of each parameter. Right: dimensionless elasticities, where the β and c curves coincide exactly (c is dashed so the overlap is visible). ::: ::: ### Global sensitivity Local derivatives can miss interactions and changes in ranking away from $p_0$. GlobalSensitivity evaluates a scalar output over a specified parameter box. Here the output is the peak infectious population. `samples=32` keeps the example short; a production analysis needs a convergence study over larger designs and, ideally, uncertainty distributions justified by data. The difference is not academic: at 32 samples the first-order index for $c$ below comes out near $0.19$, while a 16384-sample design puts it at about $0.26$. The peak is read from the solver's dense output on a fine grid rather than from daily save points, because the maximum rarely falls on a whole day: at the baseline the daily grid gives about $158.09$ on day 18, while the continuous peak is about $158.45$ near $t=17.5$. That gap is small, but it is a discretization artifact of the output definition, and it would enter every sample of the Sobol design. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function peak_infectious(p) problem = ODEProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), Float64.(p)) solution = solve(problem, Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8) # Dense interpolation on a sub-daily grid, since the peak falls between days. return maximum(solution(t)[2] for t in 0.0:0.05:40.0) end parameter_bounds = [ [0.02, 0.08], # β [5.0, 15.0], # c [0.15, 0.40], # γ ] sobol = gsa(peak_infectious, Sobol(), parameter_bounds; samples = 32) sobol_first = sobol.S1 sobol_total = sobol.ST sobol_first, sobol_total ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ([0.34941365063716207, 0.18738829410538163, 0.29222599720970627], [0.4910193351526865, 0.2979370721493215, 0.31440194330119803]) ``` ::: ::: `S1` measures the first-order contribution and `ST` includes interactions. The plot is a compact way to compare the two summaries rather than treating one ranking as universal. These indices assume independent uniform inputs over the stated bounds, and they attribute output variance under exactly that assumed distribution. Separate indices for $\beta$ and $c$ therefore quantify variance attribution under an artificial factorization of $\beta c$ into two independently sampled factors: their relative sizes follow from the widths of the two boxes chosen above, and they do not imply that incidence data can identify the two parameters separately. Sobol analysis answers "which input ranges drive the spread of this output", not "which parameters can be estimated" — that second question is the structural one taken up next. ::: {#cell-fig-ch10-global-sensitivity .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (800, 450)) ax = Axis( fig[1, 1], xticks = (1:3, ["β", "c", "γ"]), ylabel = "Sobol index", title = "Global sensitivity of the peak", ) barplot!(ax, (1:3) .- 0.18, sobol_first, width = 0.32, color = :steelblue) barplot!(ax, (1:3) .+ 0.18, sobol_total, width = 0.32, color = :darkorange) Legend(fig[1, 2], [PolyElement(color = :steelblue), PolyElement(color = :darkorange)], ["first order", "total"]) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch10-global-sensitivity .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` First-order and total Sobol indices for the infectious peak, under independent uniform sampling over the stated bounds. ::: ::: ### Structural identifiability StructuralIdentifiability uses symbolic differential algebra. We deliberately omit the known population scale in this small example to highlight the confounding of $\beta$ and $c$ in a mass-action-style observation. The package uses ASCII parameter names in this interface, so `b` and `c` stand for $\beta$ and $c$. The model below is written *symbolically*, which is a different object from the `sir_kernel!` function used above. `@parameters` and `@variables` create symbols rather than numbers; `D = Differential(t)` is a derivative operator, not a numerical difference; and `D(S) ~ -b * c * S * I` is an **equation**, where the `~` records a relationship instead of assigning a value. `ODESystem` collects those equations into a model that can be manipulated algebraically. Nothing is solved here: it is precisely because the model is symbolic that the package can reason about which parameters the observation map can distinguish, for every trajectory at once, rather than inspecting one numerical solution. ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @parameters b c g @independent_variables t @variables S(t) I(t) R(t) y(t) D = Differential(t) identifiability_system = ODESystem( [ D(S) ~ -b * c * S * I, D(I) ~ b * c * S * I - g * I, D(R) ~ g * I, ], t; name = :SIRIdentifiability, ) # Progress logging carries wall-clock timings that differ on every run. Logging.disable_logging(Logging.Info) identifiability = assess_identifiability( identifiability_system; measured_quantities = [y ~ b * c * S * I], funcs_to_check = [b, c, g, b * c], ) Logging.disable_logging(Logging.BelowMinLevel) identifiability ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` OrderedCollections.OrderedDict{Num, Symbol} with 4 entries: b => :nonidentifiable c => :nonidentifiable g => :globally b*c => :globally ``` ::: ::: The expected interpretation is that `b` and `c` are nonidentifiable while `b*c` and `g` are identifiable for this observation choice. Adding an observation that depends on one factor separately — contact-pattern data, for instance — or fixing the contact rate from external information changes the identification problem; no optimizer can recover information absent from the observation map. Note the convention: called without the `known_ic` keyword, `assess_identifiability` treats the initial conditions as generic unknown quantities, so this symbolic calculation does not use the numerical baseline initial state fixed earlier in the chapter. Declaring the initial state through `known_ic` is a separate option and a different question. It does not rescue $\beta$ and $c$ here: the map $(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,c/a)$ leaves every trajectory — and hence every observation of the states — unchanged, so the confounding persists whether or not the initial conditions are known. ## Validation The forward sensitivity solve should conserve total population, and its finite perturbation should agree with the derivative at the scale of the chosen perturbation. The elasticities of $\beta$ and $c$ should also agree to solver tolerance, since @eq-sensitivity-chain makes them equal identically. The checks below are deliberately numerical rather than asserting a particular rounded sensitivity value. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} population_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(local_states; dims = 1)) .- N)) ε = 1e-5 perturbed = copy(p0) perturbed[1] += ε perturbed_solution = solve( ODEProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), perturbed), Tsit5(); saveat = tgrid, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9, ) finite_difference = (Array(perturbed_solution)[2, end] - local_states[2, end]) / ε sensitivity_difference = abs(finite_difference - final_jacobian[2, 1]) sensitivity_relative_difference = sensitivity_difference / (1 + abs(final_jacobian[2, 1])) elasticity_gap = maximum(abs.(elasticities[1] .- elasticities[2])) @assert population_error < 1e-6 @assert sensitivity_relative_difference < 1e-3 @assert elasticity_gap < 1e-6 (population_error = population_error, sensitivity_difference = sensitivity_difference, sensitivity_relative_difference = sensitivity_relative_difference, elasticity_gap = elasticity_gap) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (population_error = 6.821210263296962e-13, sensitivity_difference = 0.8364279269455892, sensitivity_relative_difference = 0.0005394130117974082, elasticity_gap = 3.552713678800501e-15) ``` ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations The local plot describes a neighborhood of the baseline; it is not a probability distribution or a causal effect, and it is only comparable across parameters once each derivative is rescaled to the dimensionless elasticity of @eq-sensitivity-elasticity. The Sobol result is conditional on the rectangular bounds and the small quasi-random design, and it attributes variance under an assumed independent uniform distribution rather than testing whether the parameters can be estimated. Structural identifiability is an idealized, noiseless, continuous-observation result computed here under generic unknown initial conditions, whereas practical identifiability also depends on observation times, measurement error, initial conditions, and model misspecification. In particular, a fit of $\beta c$ does not justify separate biological claims about $\beta$ and $c$. The SciMLSensitivity, GlobalSensitivity, and StructuralIdentifiability APIs used here are documented in their current official links above; the computations intentionally remain small enough to inspect and rerun. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch12-ex1} Change `peak_infectious` to return the final removed count instead of the infectious peak. Re-run the Sobol calculation with the same bounds, compare the first-order and total indices, and explain why the ranking can differ between a transient output and a cumulative output. ### Exercise 2 {#ch12-ex2} Extend `identifiability_system` with an observable `n(t) ~ S + I + R`, keeping the generic unknown initial conditions of the section above — the total is informative only under that convention, since a fully specified initial state would already fix it. Assess `[b, c, g, b*c]` again. State which confounding remains, if any, and describe one additional data stream that would make the separate contact rate credible. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/12-sensitivity-and-identifiability.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/12-sensitivity-and-identifiability.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/12-sensitivity-and-identifiability.jl)
